shared.subject: Mathematics
shared.standard_text: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
shared.anchor_task: Grocery Store Showdown: FreshMart and ValueGro advertise deals on the same five items. For each item, find the price for 1 (the unit price) at both stores, decide which store wins that item, and crown the overall winner.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two quantities, written a:b.
A ratio comparing quantities in different units, like dollars and bottles.
The amount of one quantity for exactly 1 of the other.
A unit rate for money — the cost of 1 item or 1 unit of measure.

misconceptions.what: Writes a rate for a group, like '$3.60 per 2 packs', and treats it as a unit price.
misconceptions.why: 'Per' has not been anchored to 'for exactly 1' yet.
misconceptions.move: Ask: how much for exactly 1? Point to the 1 row of a ratio table.

misconceptions.what: Picks the lowest sticker price as the best deal (the $3.50 rice bag).
misconceptions.why: Compares one quantity and ignores how much each price buys.
misconceptions.move: Ask how much each price buys, then how to compare for the same amount.

misconceptions.what: Stalls when the division is uneven (3 sticks for $2.00).
misconceptions.why: Shaky fraction-as-division understanding; expects whole-number answers.
misconceptions.move: Suggest converting to cents, or scaling the ratio down by friendly numbers first.

problems.text: **Granola bars.** FreshMart: 6 bars for $3.00. ValueGro: 8 bars for $3.60. Find the price per bar at each store. Which store wins?
**Juice.** FreshMart: 4 bottles for $6.00. ValueGro: 5 bottles for $8.00. Find the price per bottle at each store. Which store wins?
**Rice.** FreshMart: a 2-pound bag for $3.50. ValueGro: a 5-pound bag for $8.00. Tomas says FreshMart wins because $3.50 is less money. Do you agree? Use unit prices to back up your answer.
**Cheese sticks.** FreshMart: 3 sticks for $2.00. ValueGro: 5 sticks for $3.50. Find the price per stick at each store. (Stuck? Try thinking in cents.) Which store wins?
**Apples.** ValueGro: 4 pounds for $6.00. Find both unit rates: dollars per pound AND pounds per dollar. Which one would help a shopper on a budget, and what does the other one tell you?

look_fors.name: Divides to find the price per 1
look_fors.what_it_means: Efficient unit-price strategy — the target of the lesson.
look_fors.teacher_move: Ask what the quotient means in context; star them to share second in Discuss.

look_fors.name: Scales a ratio table down to 1, or compares at a common amount
look_fors.teacher_move: Star them to share first in Discuss, then connect their table to a divider's shortcut.

look_fors.name: Compares only totals or only counts
look_fors.teacher_move: Ask: how much does each price buy? How could you compare for the same amount?

look_fors.name: Stalls on the cheese sticks (uneven division)
look_fors.what_it_means: Shaky fraction-as-division understanding, not a ratio problem.
look_fors.teacher_move: Offer the cents conversion or a build-down ratio table from the scaffold card.

sentence_frames: The unit price at ______ is ______ per ______.
______ is the better deal because for 1 ______ you pay ______.
I found the price for 1 by dividing ______ by ______.

exit_ticket.prompt: Store A sells a 4-bag pack of popcorn for $5.00. Store B sells a 3-bag pack for $4.20. Maya says Store B is the better deal because $4.20 is less money. Find the price per bag at each store. Who is right, and why? Use the word 'per' in your answer.

buckets.label: Got it
buckets.criteria: Both unit prices correct ($1.25 and $1.40 per bag), picks Store A, and explains using per-1 language.

buckets.label: Almost there
buckets.criteria: Divides to find a price per bag (right method) but makes an arithmetic slip or finds only one unit price; conclusion follows their numbers.

buckets.label: Needs re-teaching
buckets.criteria: Agrees with Maya by comparing totals ($4.20 < $5.00) or compares bag counts, without finding any price per bag.

blocks.label: Grade-level boundary
blocks.text: CCSS limits Grade 6 unit rates to non-complex fractions; every price in this lesson divides to a money amount or a simple fraction.

blocks.label: Mathematical practices
blocks.text: MP2: Reason abstractly and quantitatively. MP6: Attend to precision.

blocks.label: Big idea
blocks.text: A unit rate makes two deals comparable because both are priced for the same amount: exactly 1.

blocks.label: Students will be able to
items: Write a ratio a:b as a unit rate a/b
Identify real-world ratios and use them to find unit rates
Use rate language — per, for each 1 — to describe a ratio relationship

blocks.label: Prerequisites
blocks.text: 6.RP.A.1 (ratio concept and language) — students can read and write ratios. The fraction scaffold leans on 5.NF.B.3 (a fraction is division: a/b = a ÷ b) for students still shaky on fractions.

Display two bottled-water deals side by side: 2 bottles for $3.00 and 4 bottles for $5.00. Students vote on gut instinct for the better deal, then turn-and-talk to write one math question that would settle it for sure.

blocks.label: Do not resolve yet
blocks.text: Collect questions and amplify any version of 'How much does 1 bottle cost?' — the vote gets settled at the end of the mini-lesson.

items: Define ratio, rate, unit rate, unit price, per on the anchor chart
Model the water deals in a ratio table: $3.00 : 2 bottles → divide both by 2 → $1.50 : 1
Show the shortcut: unit price = price ÷ quantity, so $5.00 ÷ 4 = $1.25 per bottle
Resolve the vote: 4 for $5.00 wins at $1.25 per bottle
Quick check on whiteboards: 5 markers for $4.00 — price per marker? ($0.80)

blocks.text: Pairs work through the five Showdown items on the student handout. Every answer must use the word 'per'. Scaffold cards sit face-down on each table for any pair to flip.
Fraction scaffold (for students shaky on fractions)

rows: Student cannot see a path to 1
Divide both columns by the same friendly number until the count hits 1
a ÷ b = a/b, so $2.00 ÷ 3 sticks = 2/3 dollar per stick
Begin with items 1-2; flag item 4 as the 'cents trick' problem

blocks.text: Run a partner compare (pairs swap answers for items 3 and 4 with a neighboring pair, agree or disagree), then a whole-class share. From your observation notes, sequence a ratio-table scaler first, then a divider, and connect the two strategies.

blocks.label: Discourse questions
items: Where does the 1 live in each strategy?
Why did the $3.50 rice bag lose, even though it costs less money?
What did you do when the cheese-stick division did not come out even?
Two different unit rates describe the apples — what does each one tell you?

blocks.text: Record each Showdown item on the anchor chart as given ratio → rate per 1, and ask which column makes the comparison instant and why. Land the big idea: unit rates are comparable because both deals are priced for exactly 1, and division gets you there fast.

blocks.label: Cap the mini-lesson at 7 minutes
blocks.text: Students must do the comparing themselves in the Showdown; if direct instruction grows, Explore and Discuss shrink and the thinking transfers back to you.

blocks.label: Keep the traps
blocks.text: The rice item and the exit ticket are the only items that catch 'cheapest sticker price = best deal'. Remove them and every student looks proficient.

blocks.label: Protect the 10-minute Discuss
blocks.text: Connecting the ratio-table path to the division shortcut is where 'per 1' consolidates; cutting it leaves division as a trick without meaning.
